title: The New Neighbour
author: Barashada Ingiriisiga
description: Amina and her family start a new life in a new city, and a kind neighbour helps them find their way.

chapters.title: The New Apartment
chapters.text:
The van stopped outside a tall, grey building. Amina looked out of the window. The street was busy. She saw shops, cars, and many people. She felt a little scared. This was their new home. Her father, Youssef, paid the driver. Then he opened the big door of the building. The family carried their bags up the stairs. It was a long climb to the third floor.

The apartment was small. There was a living room, a small kitchen, and two bedrooms. The rooms were empty. The floor was clean, but the walls were white and bare. Amina’s mother, Fatima, sighed. “It is very quiet here,” she said softly. Amina looked at the window. She could see the roofs of other buildings. She could hear the city noise. It was all new.

They were all tired. Youssef put the bags down in the living room. Amina sat on the floor next to her little brother, Sami. Sami was five years old. He was sleepy and a little unhappy. “Where is my room?” he asked. Amina pointed to the small bedroom. “That is your room,” she said. Her voice was not sure.

Then they heard a knock at the door. Youssef opened it. An older man stood there. He had grey hair and a kind, round face. He smiled at them. “Hello,” he said. “I am Mr. Okoro. I live in the apartment next to you. I saw your van. Welcome to the building.”

Fatima smiled. “Thank you. I am Fatima. This is my husband, Youssef, and my children, Amina and Sami.” Mr. Okoro nodded. “You look very tired,” he said. “Moving is hard work. Do you need anything?”

Youssef shook his head. “No, thank you. We are okay.” But Mr. Okoro looked at them. He saw their empty kitchen. “I have a little time,” he said. “Come. I can show you the market. It is very near. You can buy food for tonight.” Fatima looked at Youssef. Youssef looked at the children. Then he smiled. “Okay,” he said. “Thank you. That is very kind.”

They walked with Mr. Okoro down the stairs and out into the street. The city was loud and bright. Mr. Okoro walked slowly. He pointed to a small street on the left. “The market is there,” he said. “It is open every day. You can find fruit, vegetables, and bread.” They walked into the market. The smells were wonderful. Sami smiled. Amina looked at the big piles of oranges and tomatoes. She felt a little better. Mr. Okoro helped them buy some bread and milk. Then they walked back to the apartment.

Inside, Fatima put the bread on the table. Youssef smiled at Mr. Okoro. “Thank you for your help,” he said. Mr. Okoro laughed. “You are welcome,” he said. “You are my neighbours now. We help each other here.” He said goodbye and went to his door.

Amina looked around the small, quiet apartment. It was still empty. But now, she knew the way to the market. And she knew a friendly name: Mr. Okoro. She smiled. Maybe this new city was not so bad.

chapters.title: The Clinic and the Mosque
chapters.text:
Three days passed. Amina's family began to feel more at home. The apartment was small, but it was clean and warm. Amina liked the big window in her room. She could see the street below.

But on the fourth day, Amina's mother felt sick. Her head hurt, and she was very tired. She stayed in bed all morning.

"I need to see a doctor," she said.

Amina's father looked worried. "But we do not know where the clinic is," he said.

"I can help," said a voice at the door. It was Mr. Okoro. He smiled kindly. "I will take you to the clinic. It is not far from here."

So they walked together. Amina held her mother's hand. The streets were busy. Cars and buses passed by. Mr. Okoro walked slowly so everyone could follow.

Soon they arrived at a white building. There was a red sign on the door. It said "Clinic."

Inside, it was quiet and cool. A kind nurse spoke to them. She asked Amina's mother some questions. Then a doctor came. He was a young man with a friendly face.

"Don't worry," the doctor said. "You are tired. That is all. You need rest and good food."

He gave them some medicine. Amina's mother smiled. She felt better already.

"Thank you," she said.

When they left the clinic, Mr. Okoro said, "Now I will show you the mosque. It is near here. We can pray together."

They walked for a short time. Then Amina saw a beautiful building with a tall tower. It was the mosque. The door was big and wooden. Inside, there were soft carpets and a quiet feeling.

Many people were there. Some were praying. Some were reading. Amina and her family sat down. Mr. Okoro sat next to them.

They prayed together. Amina closed her eyes. She thought about her new home, her new city, and her new friend, Mr. Okoro.

When they finished, Amina felt calm. Her heart was quiet. She was not afraid anymore.

"Thank you, Mr. Okoro," she said. "You are very kind."

"It is my pleasure," he said. "You are my neighbours now. We help each other in this city."

On the way home, Amina looked at the streets again. The cars did not seem so noisy now. The buildings did not seem so tall. The city felt like home.

Her mother walked more slowly, but she was smiling. Amina was grateful. She had a new home, a new friend, and a place to pray.

That night, Amina slept very well.

chapters.title: The Market and Tea
chapters.text:
On Saturday morning, Mr. Okoro knocked on their door. "Today is market day," he said with a big smile. "Come with me. You will see many good things."

Amina's mother smiled. "Thank you, Mr. Okoro. We need many things for the house."

They walked together through the busy streets. The market was very big. There were many colours and sounds. People called out and laughed. The smell of fresh bread and fruit filled the air.

Mr. Okoro showed them the vegetable seller first. There were big red tomatoes, green peppers, and long yellow bananas. Amina's mother touched the tomatoes carefully. "These are very fresh," she said.

The vegetable seller laughed. "I pick them every morning," she said.

They bought tomatoes, onions, and some green beans. Then Mr. Okoro took them to the bread shop. The bread was warm and soft. Amina held the bag close to her face and smelled it. "Mmm," she said. "It smells so good."

Her father laughed. "You are hungry, Amina?"

"Yes, Papa," she said. "Very hungry."

Mr. Okoro looked at them. "Then you must come to my home. I have tea, and my wife made some honey cakes this morning."

Amina's eyes opened wide. "Honey cakes?"

"Yes, little one," Mr. Okoro said. "The best in the city."

They followed him to his apartment. It was small, like theirs, but very warm and bright. His wife, Mrs. Okoro, was waiting at the door. She welcomed them with open arms.

"Come in, come in," she said. "Sit down. Rest your feet."

The tea was hot and sweet. Amina drank it slowly. The honey cakes were soft and golden. She ate two of them. Mrs. Okoro smiled at her.

"You like them?" she asked.

"Yes," Amina said. "They are the best I have ever had."

Everyone laughed. The room was full of warm light and good smells. Amina looked around her. Here, in this new city, in this small apartment, she felt something new. She felt safe. She felt happy.

She thought about the first day, when everything was strange and scary. Now the market was a friendly place. The clinic was near. The mosque was beautiful. And Mr. and Mrs. Okoro were like family.

Amina smiled into her tea. Maybe this new city was not so strange after all. Maybe it was the beginning of a good life.
